unit.unitTitle: Block It Out: Moving from Blocks to Text
unit.unitOverview: Hello, and welcome to your very first unit of Year 7 Computing! In this unit you will make an exciting jump. Up to now, you have probably built programs by dragging and dropping coloured blocks in Scratch. That is called block-based programming. In this unit you will move on to text-based programming, where you write real code by typing it, letter by letter, using a language called Python. Python is one of the most widely used programming languages in the whole world. It runs websites, games, robots, phone apps, and even the computers that scientists use to study space and weather. The best part is that Python is completely free, and you can install it on almost any computer. By the end of this unit, you will be writing your own Python programs that talk to the user, do calculations, and give back answers, just like a calculator does. The big idea of this unit is simple: the ideas you already know from Scratch still work in Python. A program still runs step by step (this is called sequencing). It still uses variables to remember things. It still asks the user questions and shows answers. It still makes choices using IF and ELSE. What changes is only the way you write it: instead of clicking blocks together, you now type the instructions as text. Once you see how the blocks match the text, the change feels much smaller than you expect.

concepts.title: Block-Based vs Text-Based Programming
concepts.explanation:
There are hundreds of programming languages in the world, but most fall into two families. Block-based languages, like Scratch, let you build programs by snapping blocks together, like building bricks. You do not have to remember any code, you just pick the block you want. This makes them wonderful for getting started.

Text-based languages, like Python, are different. There are no blocks to drag. Instead, you type the instructions yourself. This means you have to remember the syntax (the exact way the code must be written), and you have to spell everything correctly. It feels harder at first, but it is far more powerful, and it is how professional software is really made.

Here is the encouraging truth: the ideas are the same in both. Look at how a Scratch block matches a line of Python:

Because the ideas match, everything you learned in Scratch gives you a head start in Python. You are not starting from zero, you are translating skills you already have.

Scratch block — Python code · What it does

say [Hello world] — print("Hello world") · Show a message on screen

set [score] to (0) — score = 0 · Put a value into a variable

ask [What is your name?] — name = input("What is your name? ") · Get input from the user

concepts.title: Meet Thonny, Your Python Workshop
concepts.explanation:
To write Python, you need a program that lets you type code, run it, and see the results. A program like this is called an IDE (Integrated Development Environment). The one we use at Ehel Academy is Thonny. It is free, open-source, and was designed especially for beginners by a university in Estonia. Best of all, Thonny comes with Python already inside it, so you only install one thing.

Go to thonny.org, download Thonny for your computer (Windows, Mac or Linux), and install it. There are full step-by-step instructions in your Reference document, so follow those the first time. Once it is installed, open Thonny. You will see a window split into two main parts:

The Editor (the large area at the top). This is where you type and save full programs. This is called script mode.

The Shell (the smaller area at the bottom). This is where Python talks back to you, shows output, and where you can type quick single commands. This is interactive mode.

You will use both parts. Think of the Editor as your notebook where you write a whole recipe, and the Shell as the kitchen counter where you can quickly taste one ingredient. Let us start in the Shell.
concepts.example: Thonny was created at the University of Tartu in Estonia to help students learn Python. It has a special 'Variables' window that lets you watch your variables change as your program runs, which is a fantastic way to understand what your code is really doing.

concepts.title: The Shell and the print() Statement
concepts.explanation:
Click into the Shell at the bottom of Thonny. You will see the prompt >>>. This prompt means Python is waiting for you to type a command. When you press ENTER, Python runs your command straight away. This is interactive mode, perfect for quick experiments.

The most important command to learn first is print(). The print statement displays whatever you put inside its brackets on the screen. Text (a string) must go inside quotation marks. Type this next to the >>> prompt and press ENTER:

The words appear, but the quotation marks do not. That is because the quotation marks are only there to tell Python where your text starts and ends. Now try a calculation. In the Shell, you do not even need print() for sums, just type the calculation:
concepts.example: Notice the * symbol means multiply in Python (not the letter x). Python worked out 7 + 6 = 13 first because it was in brackets, then multiplied by 2 to get 26. You have just used the shell as a calculator!

concepts.title: Python Is Fussy - Case and Syntax
concepts.explanation:
Python is case sensitive. This means it treats capital letters and small letters as completely different. The command is print with a small p. If you type Print with a capital P, Python will not understand it and will show an error. Try it in the Shell:

Type this (it will cause an error on purpose):

NameError: name 'Print' is not defined

Do not panic when you see an error, this is a normal part of programming! The message is Python's way of saying 'I do not know a command called Print'. The fix is simple: use a small p. Always type Python commands in lower case.

Another very common error is forgetting a quotation mark or a bracket. The exact rules of how code must be written are called the syntax. If your syntax is wrong, Python shows a syntax error. For example, this line is missing the closing quotation mark:

SyntaxError: unterminated string literal
concepts.example: The fix is to add the missing quotation mark so the text has one at the start and one at the end: print("Hello world"). Two useful shell commands to remember: type help(print) to read how print works, and type exit() to close the shell.

concepts.title: Writing and Saving a Program (Script Mode)
concepts.explanation: The shell is great for quick tests, but there is one big problem: you cannot save what you type there. Real programs have many lines and need to be saved and run again later. For that, you use the Editor (script mode). Follow these steps in Thonny to make your first saved program: Click File, then New (or press Ctrl+N). A blank editor opens at the top. Type your program into the editor (see the code below). Click File, then Save (or press Ctrl+S). Give it the name HelloWorld — Thonny adds .py automatically, because .py is the ending for every Python file. Click the green Run button (or press F5). Your program runs, and the output appears in the Shell below. Type this into Thonny's editor: I am learning Python at Ehel Academy
concepts.example: See how the three lines run in order, from top to bottom? This is sequencing, and it is one of the most important ideas in programming. The computer does exactly what you tell it, in exactly the order you write it. If you ever need to change a saved program, use File > Open, edit it, and save again.

concepts.title: Variables - The Computer's Memory Boxes
concepts.explanation:
A variable is a named box in the computer's memory that stores a value. You put a value into a variable using the = sign. The name goes on the left, the value goes on the right. Here are four variables that store details about a student:

Notice that text values (strings) go inside quotation marks, but numbers do not. Once a value is stored, you can display it. To show the name variable, you put its name inside print(). Do not put quotation marks around a variable name, or Python will print the word instead of the stored value.

Type this into Thonny's editor:

Look carefully: we put a comma between the text "Your name is" and the variable name. The comma joins them together in the output, and Python automatically adds one space where the comma is. Let us display the age too:

Type this into Thonny's editor:

The word variable means 'able to vary', in other words, its value can change while the program runs. That is what makes variables so powerful: the same program can work with different values each time it runs.

Variables are not only used in programming. Spreadsheets use them too, but they are called cell references there. Scientists use variables to model the weather, predict floods, and study money markets. A variable is simply a name for a value that might change.

concepts.title: Data Types - String, Integer and Real (Float)
concepts.explanation:
Every piece of data in Python has a data type. The three you need for this unit are:

In Python, the 'real' data type is called float, which is short for 'floating point number'. You will use integers for things you count in whole numbers (like a person's age or a number of trees), and floats for things that can have decimals (like money, or a length in metres).

There is one very important rule to remember about input(): the input() function always gives back a string, even if the user types a number. If the user types 5, Python stores it as the text "5", not the number 5. This causes a famous beginner bug, which we fix in the next step.

Data type — What it stores · Examples

String — Text: letters, numbers or symbols in quotes · "Hello", "WE5694", "Leila"

Integer (int) — A whole number, with no decimal point · 24, 0, -10
concepts.example: Real / Float — A number with a decimal point · 6.98, 3.5, -0.04

concepts.title: Casting - Turning Text into Numbers
concepts.explanation:
Because input() always gives a string, you cannot do maths with it directly. Watch what goes wrong. This program is meant to double a number:

Type this into Thonny's editor:

If the user types 5, you might expect the answer 10. But look what actually happens:

Instead of 10, we got 55! Why? Because num1 is the string "5", and multiplying a string by 2 just repeats the text: "5" + "5" = "55". Python did not add, it copied the text twice. To fix this, we must tell Python 'treat this input as a whole number'. Changing data to the correct type is called casting.

To cast to an integer, wrap the input in int(). To cast to a float (decimal), wrap it in float():

Type this into Thonny's editor:

Now it works! Remember this rule for the rest of the unit: if you want to do maths with an input, you must cast it with int() or float(). Forgetting to cast is the number one cause of wrong answers for beginners.

Code — What it does

num1 = int(input("Enter a number: ")) — Stores the input as a whole number (integer)
concepts.example: num1 = float(input("Enter a number: ")) — Stores the input as a decimal number (float)

concepts.title: Planning with Algorithms and Flowcharts
concepts.explanation:
Before writing code, good programmers plan. A plan written as a set of ordered steps is an algorithm. A popular way to draw an algorithm is a flowchart, which uses standard symbols:

Here is the flowchart for the addition program from our scenario. Read it from top to bottom:

[ OUTPUT ] "The total of the two numbers is", total

Once the flowchart is planned, turning it into Python is straightforward, you just get the syntax right:

Type this into Thonny's editor:

The total of the two numbers is 35

Symbol — What it is used for

Start / Stop — An oval. Marks the beginning and the end.

Input / Output — A parallelogram. Getting data in, or showing data out.

Process — A rectangle. A step where something is worked out.
concepts.example: Decision — A diamond. A question with two answers (Yes / No).

concepts.title: Selection - Making Choices with IF ... ELSE
concepts.explanation:
Sometimes a program must choose what to do. This is called selection, and it happens when the program checks a condition (something that is true or false). In a flowchart, selection uses the decision diamond. To compare values, you use comparison operators:

Be careful: to compare two values you use == (two equals signs). A single = is only for storing a value in a variable. Mixing these up is a very common mistake.

Here is a scenario: a user enters two test scores. If the total is over 100, show 'Well done', otherwise show 'Better luck next time'. First, the flowchart:

+--- NO ---> [ OUTPUT ] "Better luck next time"

Now the same idea in Python. Notice the colon (:) at the end of the if and else lines, and notice that the lines underneath are indented (pushed in). Thonny adds this indent for you automatically after a colon. The indent tells Python which lines belong to the choice.

Type this into Thonny's editor:

Operator — Meaning

== — equal to

!= — not equal to

< — less than

> — greater than

<= — less than or equal to

concepts.title: Sub-Routines - Mini-Programs Inside Programs
concepts.explanation:
As programs grow, they can become confusing. A sub-routine is a small, named mini-program inside your program that does one job. You can 'call' it whenever you need it, and you can reuse it as many times as you like. This keeps your main program tidy and easy to follow.

In Python, you create a sub-routine with the word def (short for 'define'), followed by a name and brackets. Here is a calculator that uses two sub-routines, one for adding and one for subtracting, and uses selection to choose which to run:

Type this into Thonny's editor:

Enter 1 to add or 2 to subtract: 1
concepts.example: The (a, b) after each sub-routine name are the two numbers we hand over for it to work with. When we call addition(number1, number2), the sub-routine receives our two numbers and does its job. If the user had entered 2, the subtract sub-routine would run instead and give 4. If they entered anything else, the program politely asks for a valid number. This is exactly how Mr Karim's calculator can offer many operations in one neat program.

terms: text-based programming
Programming where you type the code as text, using a language such as Python.
block-based programming
Programming by dragging and dropping blocks that snap together, as in Scratch.
Python
A popular, free, text-based programming language. You will use it all through this unit.
IDE (Integrated Development Environment)
A program that helps you write, save, test and run code. Thonny and IDLE are both Python IDEs.
Python shell
Python's interactive mode, where you type one command and see the result straight away.
interactive mode
A way of using Python where each command is run immediately in the shell.
script mode
Python's editor, where you type a list of commands, save them as a file, and run them together.
print statement
A Python command that outputs text or values onto the screen.
string
Data made of letters, numbers or symbols, written inside quotation marks, e.g. "Hello".
integer
A whole number, such as 24 or -10.
real / float
A number with a decimal point, such as 6.98. Python calls this data type float.
variable
A named place in the computer's memory that stores a value; the value can change as the program runs.
input function
A Python function that captures what the user types. It always gives back a string.
casting
Changing data to the correct data type, for example with int() or float().
data type
The kind of data being stored, such as string, integer or float.
arithmetic operator
A symbol used for calculations: + - * / and others.
BIDMAS
The order maths is done: Brackets, Indices, Division, Multiplication, Addition, Subtraction.
syntax
The exact structure and spelling rules of a programming language.
comment
A note in the code that starts with # and is ignored by Python; it explains the code.
interpreter
The part of Python that translates your code into machine code, line by line.
machine code
The language of 0s and 1s that the computer actually carries out.
case sensitive
Treating capital and small letters as different, so Print is not the same as print.
execute / run
To make the computer carry out your program.
algorithm
A sequence of steps or instructions to solve a problem.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: In your own words, what is the difference between block-based and text-based programming?
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: Block-based programming (like Scratch) uses drag-and-drop blocks that snap together, so you do not type code. Text-based programming (like Python) means you type the code yourself and must follow the exact syntax. The ideas are the same; only the way you write them differs.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: What is the difference between the Python shell (interactive mode) and the editor (script mode)?
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: The shell (interactive mode) runs one command at a time, straight away, and cannot be saved. The editor (script mode) lets you type many lines, save them as a .py file, and run them together.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: Why must you use int() or float() on an input before doing a calculation with it?
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: Because input() always returns a string. If you do maths on a string you get the wrong result (like "5" * 2 giving "55") or an error. Casting with int() or float() turns it into a number so calculations work.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: Give one example each of a string, an integer and a float.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: Examples: a string is "Leila"; an integer is 12; a float is 3.5. (Any sensible examples are correct.)

reasoningPrompts.prompt: What is the difference between = and == in Python?
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: A single = stores (assigns) a value in a variable, e.g. age = 12. A double == compares two values to see if they are equal, e.g. if age == 12.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: What does a comment (#) do, and why is it useful?
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: A comment starts with # and is ignored by Python. It is a note for humans that explains what the code does, which makes the program easier to read and fix.
